\section[urbs, urbis]{urbs, urbis — a city}

\label{lesson:LA-C107-urbs}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for a hundred, then the Latin for a thousand.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: urbs, urbis}
\textbf{urbs, urbis} — \textquotedblleft{}a city\textquotedblright{}. English \emph{urban}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{urbs} has no sure origin; no proposal is generally accepted.
\end{cousinweb}

\section[oppidum, oppidī]{oppidum, oppidī — a town}

\label{lesson:LA-C107-oppidum}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for a thousand, then the Latin for a city.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: oppidum, oppidī}
\textbf{oppidum, oppidī} — \textquotedblleft{}a town\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{oppidum} is usually explained as \emph{ob}, \textquotedblleft{}on, over\textquotedblright{}, and a word for \textquotedblleft{}ground, place\textquotedblright{}, the one in Greek \emph{pedon}, \textquotedblleft{}ground\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\section[forum, forī]{forum, forī — a forum, a market square}

\label{lesson:LA-C107-forum}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for a city, then the Latin for a town.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: forum, forī}
\textbf{forum, forī} — \textquotedblleft{}a forum, a market square\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{forum} is usually traced to Proto-Indo-European \emph{*dhworom}, \textquotedblleft{}enclosure\textquotedblright{}, from \emph{*dhwer-}, \textquotedblleft{}door\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB 2.1); \emph{forās}, \textquotedblleft{}out of doors\textquotedblright{}, and English \emph{door} belong to the same family.
\end{cousinweb}

One more word for this chapter.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[templum, templī]{templum, templī — a temple}

\label{lesson:LA-C107-templum}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for a town, then the Latin for a forum.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: templum, templī}
\textbf{templum, templī} — \textquotedblleft{}a temple\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{templum} first meant a space marked out for watching the sky. Its origin is uncertain: Lewis \& Short link it with Greek \emph{temnō}, \textquotedblleft{}to cut\textquotedblright{}, and \emph{temenos}, \textquotedblleft{}a sacred precinct\textquotedblright{}; EtymDB 2.1 traces it to a root \emph{*temp-}, \textquotedblleft{}to stretch\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\section[taberna, tabernae]{taberna, tabernae — a shop, an inn}

\label{lesson:LA-C107-taberna}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for a forum, then the Latin for a temple.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: taberna, tabernae}
\textbf{taberna, tabernae} — \textquotedblleft{}a shop, an inn\textquotedblright{}. English \emph{tavern}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{taberna} has no sure origin; one common view derives it from \emph{trabs}, \textquotedblleft{}a beam\textquotedblright{}: a hut of planks.
\end{cousinweb}
